title: Reproduction in Plants
summary: Reproduction is the production of one's own kind. Vegetative reproduction: a vegetative part (root, stem, leaf or bud) detaches and grows into a new plant; offspring are clones (mitosis only). Fragmentation: filament of Spirogyra breaks into pieces that grow. Fission (bacteria, yeast: binary or multiple) and budding (yeast). Asexual reproduction by spores (bread mould, moss, fern; flagellate zoospores or non-flagellate spores); higher plants are heterosporous (microspores and megaspores formed by meiosis). Sexual reproduction: fusion of haploid male and female gametes (fertilisation) to form a diploid zygote; offspring are genetically different. Apomixis: seeds formed without fertilisation from a diploid cell of the ovule (dandelion); an asexual process that disperses seeds.

Chlamydomonas: haploid, unicellular, pear-shaped alga with two flagella, an eyespot, a cup-shaped chloroplast with a pyrenoid. Asexual reproduction: zoospores (when water is plentiful: 2-16 flagellate daughter protoplasts), aplanospores (palmella stage, in a thin film of water) and hypnospores (thick-walled, on drying). Sexual reproduction: isogamy (gametes identical in structure but different physiologically, e.g. C. eugametos), anisogamy (female gametes larger, e.g. C. braunii) and oogamy (non-motile egg and motile male gametes, e.g. C. coccifera). The zygote is the only diploid stage; it forms a thick-walled zygospore and on germination divides by meiosis into four haploid zoospores. Spirogyra: filamentous green alga with spiral ribbon-shaped chloroplasts with pyrenoids. Vegetative reproduction by fragmentation; sexual reproduction by conjugation: scalariform (two filaments lie parallel and cells pair through conjugation tubes, ladder-like; the gamete of the male filament passes by amoeboid movement into the female cell, forming a zygospore) and lateral (cells of the same filament; alternating male and female cells). Zygospore germinates by meiosis forming four haploid nuclei, three degenerate and one gives a new filament.

Angiosperms are annual (pea), biennial (radish) or perennial (mango, neem); monocarpic (flower once, e.g. bamboo, agave, annuals) or polycarpic (flower many times, e.g. mango). The juvenile phase (soft stem, few leaves, no flowering) gives way to the adult phase when the vegetative shoot apex becomes a floral apex. Factors affecting flowering: temperature (vernalisation: low temperature treatment stimulates early flowering) and light (photoperiodism). Sex in flowers: bisexual or unisexual; chromosomal (XX and XY in some dioecious species) and hormonal (gibberellin promotes male flowers in Cucumis; auxin and ethylene promote female flowers).

Stamen: anther with four pollen sacs (microsporangia) with wall layers epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum (innermost, nourishes pollen grains); microspore mother cells divide by meiosis into four haploid microspores (tetrad), each develops into a pollen grain (male gametophyte) with outer exine (sporopollenin, with germ pores) and inner intine; the nucleus divides into a vegetative (tube) cell and a generative cell, which forms two male gametes; the pollen grain is not itself the male gamete.

Pistil: ovary with ovules; ovule has nucellus, two integuments, micropyle, chalaza and funiculus. A megaspore mother cell divides by meiosis giving four megaspores (three degenerate); the functional megaspore divides three times by mitosis giving 8 nuclei in the embryo sac: egg apparatus at the micropylar end (egg and two synergids), three antipodal cells at the chalazal end and two polar nuclei in the central cell, which fuse into the diploid secondary nucleus. A mature embryo sac has 8 nuclei in 7 cells. Functions: egg forms the zygote; secondary nucleus fuses with a sperm to give the triploid primary endosperm nucleus; synergids guide the pollen tube; antipodals nourish the young embryo.

Pollination: transfer of pollen from anther to stigma; self-pollination (same flower or same plant; pea, gram) or cross-pollination (different plants). Agents: wind (anemophily: small, colourless flowers, light or winged pollen in large numbers, large feathery stigmas; grasses), insects (large, coloured, scented flowers with nectar; Salvia), water (Hydrilla, Vallisneria) and animals (birds, squirrels). Adaptations for cross-pollination: unisexuality (papaya, maize), dichogamy (anther and stigma mature at different times; sweet pea, custard apple) and self-sterility (apple, Petunia). Devices for self-pollination: cleistogamy (flowers remain closed) and homogamy (anther and stigma mature together; groundnut).

Fertilisation: the pollen grain germinates on the stigma; the pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle, bursts in a synergid and releases two male gametes; one fuses with the egg (syngamy) forming the diploid zygote and the other with the secondary nucleus (triple fusion) forming the triploid primary endosperm nucleus; the two fusions together are double fertilisation. Post-fertilisation: endosperm (nuclear, cellular or helobial; nuclear in maize and wheat); embryo (zygote divides into an embryonal cell and a suspensor cell; develops radicle, plumule and cotyledons); integuments become the seed coat (the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit). Polyembryony: more than one embryo in a seed (adventive from other cells of the embryo sac; cleavage from division of the zygote). Parthenocarpy: fruit development without fertilisation (banana, grapes), seedless.

Seeds: dicot (gram): testa, tegmen, hilum, micropyle, two cotyledons and embryonal axis; monocot (maize): fused testa and pericarp, endosperm with aleurone layer, one large cotyledon (scutellum), coleoptile and coleorhiza. Dormancy helps survival; germination needs water, suitable temperature and oxygen; steps: imbibition, swelling, enzyme action, radicle then plumule. Epigeal germination: cotyledons come above ground (castor, bean); hypogeal: cotyledons stay below ground (maize, rice, gram).

Natural: adventitious buds on roots (sweet potato), stems (runner, sucker, bulb, tuber, rhizome), leaf margins (Bryophyllum) and bulbils (Agave, Oxalis). Artificial: cutting (rose, sugarcane, money plant), layering (jasmine, strawberry, grapevine), aerial layering or gootee, grafting (stock and scion; rose, mango, citrus, apple) and micropropagation or tissue culture (a small piece of tissue in sterile nutrient medium forms a callus, which is moved to a hormone medium to form plantlets; orchids, carnation, chrysanthemum, asparagus). Advantages: rapid, identical offspring, perennation and cheap; disadvantages: overcrowding, no new varieties and rapid spread of disease.

objective: Fill in the blanks (any two): (a) ______ and ______ are devices that ensure self-pollination. (b) ______ and ______ are adaptations to promote cross-pollination.
(a) Cleistogamy and homogamy. (b) Dichogamy and self-sterility (also unisexuality).
Label the parts of the androecium and gynoecium (any one).
Androecium: anther (with pollen sacs), connective and filament. Gynoecium: stigma, style and ovary (with ovules).
Fill in the blank: Yeast reproduces by the ______ method.
Name the three types of sexual reproduction in Chlamydomonas.
Match: (a) Bryophyllum (b) Agave (c) Ginger with (i) bulbil (ii) leaf buds (iii) rhizome.
State true or false: (a) The pollen grain is the male gamete. (b) Apomixis involves no fertilisation.
(a) False – it is the male gametophyte. (b) True.
Name the cells of the egg apparatus and of the chalazal end.
Egg cell and two synergids; three antipodal cells.
Name the artificial methods of vegetative propagation with one example each.
Cutting (rose), layering (jasmine), grafting (mango) and tissue culture (orchids).
vsa: Differentiate between asexual and sexual reproduction (two points).
Asexual involves a single parent without fusion of gametes and the offspring are identical; sexual involves two gametes and the offspring show variation.
What is parthenocarpy? Give two examples.
Development of fruit without fertilisation, giving seedless fruits; e.g. banana and grapes.
What is polyembryony? Name its two types.
More than one embryo in a seed: adventive (from other cells of the embryo sac) and cleavage (from division of the zygote).
Low temperature treatment that stimulates early flowering in some plants.
List any four advantages of vegetative propagation.
It is rapid and cheap, the offspring are identical to the parent, food storage organs allow perennation and it ensures survival of seedless varieties.
Write the functions of synergids and antipodal cells.
Synergids guide the pollen tube to the egg; antipodals degenerate and provide nutrition to the young embryo.
Differentiate between epigeal and hypogeal germination (one example each).
In epigeal the cotyledons come above the ground (castor); in hypogeal they stay underground (maize).
Production of seeds without fertilisation from a diploid cell of the ovule (dandelion).
sa: Briefly explain double fertilisation in an angiosperm. Mention the end products formed by this process.

The pollen tube releases two sperms into the embryo sac; one fuses with the egg (syngamy) to give the diploid zygote and the other fuses with the diploid secondary nucleus (triple fusion) to give the triploid primary endosperm nucleus. End products: embryo and endosperm.
Describe the structure of the mature embryo sac.

It has seven cells and eight nuclei: an egg apparatus (egg and two synergids) at the micropylar end, three antipodal cells at the chalazal end and a large central cell with two polar nuclei that fuse to form the secondary nucleus.
Write the adaptations of wind-pollinated flowers.
Small, colourless, odourless flowers; large numbers of light or winged pollen; large, hairy and protruding stigmas.
Explain the structure of the maize grain.
It has a pericarp fused with the seed coat, an endosperm with a protein-rich aleurone layer and a single large cotyledon (scutellum), with the embryonal axis lying lateral to it.

A small piece of plant tissue is cultured in a sterile nutrient medium; it forms a callus, which on a hormone medium forms plantlets; these are transplanted; an indefinite number of identical plants can be produced.
Self-pollination is the transfer to the stigma of the same flower or plant (pea); cross-pollination is the transfer to a flower of another plant (palm, maize), producing variation.
la: Describe the development of the male gametophyte (pollen grain) in angiosperms.

The anther has four microsporangia with tapetum; microspore mother cells divide by meiosis into four microspores (tetrad); each forms a pollen grain with exine and intine; its nucleus divides into a vegetative and a generative cell, which gives two male gametes.
Describe the development of the female gametophyte (embryo sac).

A megaspore mother cell in the nucellus divides by meiosis into four megaspores; three degenerate; the functional megaspore divides three times to give eight nuclei, which form the egg apparatus, antipodals and the central cell with polar nuclei.
Explain the types of pollination and the characteristics of wind- and insect-pollinated flowers.
Self and cross pollination; wind pollinated: small, scentless flowers, light pollen, large stigma; insect pollinated: large, coloured, scented flowers with nectar and sticky pollen.
Asexual by zoospores, aplanospores and hypnospores; sexual by isogamy, anisogamy and oogamy, with a diploid zygote that undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid zoospores.
Describe the post-fertilisation changes in a flower.
Endosperm formed from the primary endosperm nucleus; embryo from the zygote with suspensor; integuments form the seed coat; the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit; fruit ripening.
Explain the artificial methods of vegetative propagation.
Cuttings, layering and aerial layering, grafting (stock and scion) and tissue culture, with examples and advantages.
